narrative.text: The Russian title page of the WHO/UNFPA guidance on preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines for national policy and programmes.
The Russian copyright and disclaimer page of the 2007 HPV vaccine guidance, with WHO Press ordering and permissions details.
The Russian table of contents of the HPV vaccine guidance, covering cervical cancer and HPV, the vaccines, target groups, advocacy, service delivery, monitoring, stewardship and financing.
The Russian acknowledgements, explaining that the guidance draws on a March 2006 technical consultation in Montreux and listing the experts, UNFPA and WHO staff, authors and WHO departments involved.

The Russian introduction, stating that the guidance aims to alert reproductive health, immunization, adolescent health and cancer programmes to key issues for introducing HPV vaccines within the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy. It describes cervical cancer as the second most common cancer in women, with about 500,000 cases and 250,000 deaths a year, mostly in low-income countries, and nearly all linked to genital HPV infection.

A Russian box on the 2005 World Health Assembly cancer resolution, which highlighted cervical cancer control and asked WHO to promote vaccine research, with a figure on HPV infection, pre-cancer and cancer prevalence by age.

Describes in Russian the two prophylactic HPV vaccines, which showed excellent efficacy against persistent infection and cervical lesions in women aged 16–24, both targeting types 16 and 18 and one also types 6 and 11. It also mentions single-visit screening with VIA and cryotherapy and a figure on HPV type distribution by region.

Reports in Russian near 100% protection against vaccine-type cervical pre-cancer and 95–99% against genital warts, with expected prevention of 70% of cervical cancers, and lists ongoing research questions on duration and special groups. It then introduces the choice of target groups, ideally before sexual debut.

Discusses in Russian other groups that might benefit from HPV vaccines, such as males, children under 9, people living with HIV and pregnant women, noting that data on efficacy, safety or cost-effectiveness are still lacking.

Links HPV vaccines in Russian to the 2004 global reproductive health strategy and its call for synergies between services, and describes the vaccines' innovative potential to strengthen links between services and prevent common cancers.

Summarises in Russian the goals of the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy to 2015 and its expansion of immunization beyond infants, and discusses the roles of cancer control and HIV programmes in HPV vaccine introduction.

Explains in Russian that HPV vaccination offers an extra chance to promote STI prevention and that success depends on cross-sector cooperation, while noting the vaccine is likely to be expensive for developing countries and that cost should not be the only decision criterion. It warns that private-sector-only introduction could widen inequities and stresses cultural sensitivities.

Notes in Russian the potential synergies between immunization, cancer and reproductive health programmes and the need for international partnerships to shorten the gap between licensing in rich countries and affordable supply to developing countries.

Describes in Russian the challenges and opportunities of HPV vaccine advocacy and communication, including balanced public education and clarifying roles across programmes, and presents the vaccines as most effective within a comprehensive strategy. It begins listing key messages about HPV and the vaccines.

Continues the Russian key messages, noting that vaccines do not protect against other STIs or HIV and that about 30% of cervical cancers will not be prevented, so screening must continue. It advises culturally sensitive messaging that does not focus only on girls and clearly explains what the vaccine can and cannot do.

Describes in Russian the information needs of key audiences, including policy-makers and providers (disease burden, programme benefits, screening methods, partnerships, financing) and adolescents and families (what HPV is and how it relates to cancer).

Discusses in Russian reaching the primary target group, likely girls aged 9–13 before sexual debut, through school-based programmes or immunization campaigns, noting limits where girls leave school early and the possibility of combining with tetanus vaccination campaigns.

Describes in Russian outreach to out-of-school youth through civil society and the secondary target group of unvaccinated women aged 14–26, whose coverage depends on resources, warning against diverting resources from the primary cohort. It also notes how reproductive health services can spread information.

Discusses in Russian building HPV vaccine delivery on existing structures such as the cold chain and partnerships across immunization, reproductive health, adolescent, cancer and HIV programmes, education and civil society. It begins the section on monitoring and evaluation.

Lists in Russian the action points for national programmes on service delivery, such as linking stakeholders, defining the primary target group, addressing sociocultural barriers, checking school attendance, updating cervical cancer strategies and developing a delivery strategy with consistent messages and health worker training.

Discusses in Russian stewardship and financing, urging resource mobilisation within broader partner strategies and health system strengthening, and noting that reproductive health programmes are well placed to advise on policy decisions. It highlights the difficulty of prioritising an expensive vaccine among competing needs.

Explains in Russian that external funding could spur national action and that without it countries must use public resources, donations or private-sector introduction. It advises aligning HPV vaccine planning with multi-year immunization plans, sector-wide approaches and GAVI funding windows.

Lists in Russian financing action points, including country demand and cost modelling based on cancer burden and HPV type data, involvement of reproductive health programmes in GAVI applications, and WHO/UNFPA technical help for non-eligible countries.

The Russian epilogue, stating that introduction decisions rest with countries, that the vaccine belongs within integrated services and partnerships, and that equity must be addressed so poorer women benefit. It also calls for guidance and protocols to support the recommended actions.
A Russian list of additional resources with web links for UNFPA, WHO, GIVS and GAVI.
